Background and Objectives The central vein sign (CVS), a central linear hypointensity within lesions on T2*-weighted imaging, has been established as a sensitive and specific biomarker for the diagnosis of multiple sclerosis (MS). However, the CVS has not yet been comprehensively studied in newly developing MS lesions. We aimed to identify the CVS profiles of new white matter lesions in patients with MS followed over time and investigate demographic and clinical risk factors associated with new CVS+ or CVS− lesion development. Methods In this retrospective longitudinal cohort study, adults from the NIH MS Natural History Study were considered for inclusion. Participants with new T2 or enhancing lesions were identified through review of the radiology report and/or longitudinal subtraction imaging. Each new lesion was evaluated for the CVS. Clinical characteristics were identified through chart review. Results A total of 153 adults (95 relapsing-remitting MS, 27 secondary progressive MS, 16 primary progressive MS, 5 clinically isolated syndrome, and 10 healthy; 67% female) were included. Of this cohort, 96 had at least 1 new T2 or contrast-enhancing lesion during median 3.1 years (Q1–Q3: 0.7–6.3) of follow-up; lesions eligible for CVS evaluation were found in 62 (65%). Of 233 new CVS-eligible lesions, 159 (68%) were CVS+, with 30 (48%) individuals having only CVS+, 12 (19%) only CVS−, and 20 (32%) both CVS+ and CVS− lesions. In gadolinium-enhancing (Gd+) lesions, the CVS+ percentage increased from 102/152 (67%) at the first time point where the lesion was observed, to 92/114 (82%) after a median follow-up of 2.8 years. Younger age (OR = 0.5 per 10-year increase, 95% CI = 0.3–0.8) and higher CVS+ percentage at baseline (OR = 1.4 per 10% increase, 95% CI = 1.1–1.9) were associated with increased likelihood of new CVS+ lesion development. Discussion In a cohort of adults with MS followed over a median duration of 3 years, most newly developing T2 or enhancing lesions were CVS+ (68%), and nearly half (48%) developed new CVS+ lesions only. Importantly, the effects of edema and T2 signal changes can obscure small veins in Gd+ lesions; therefore, caution and follow-up is necessary when determining their CVS status. Trial Registration Information Clinical trial registration number NCT00001248. Classification of Evidence This study provides Class III evidence that younger age and higher CVS+ percentage at baseline are associated with new CVS+ lesion development. OPEN-ACCESS TRUE Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic CNS disease, characterized by inflammatory demyelination and neuroaxonal loss. 1 , 2 The clinical diagnosis of MS currently relies on MRI to demonstrate evidence of lesion dissemination in space and time. 3 , 4 MRI is key to the determination of inflammatory disease activity, manifested by an increasing quantity of T2 and/or gadolinium enhancing (Gd+) white matter lesions. An increasing lesion load is associated with worsening disability progression and treatment failure in patients treated with disease-modifying therapy (DMT). 5 , 6 Despite the importance of monitoring lesion load in patients with MS, a variety of etiologies can contribute to the appearance of T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintense lesions on brain MRI that can mimic MS lesions, such as small vessel disease, migraine, inflammatory vasculopathies, and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder. 7 Increased prevalence of vascular risk factors in patients with MS has been well established in the literature, along with corresponding increased lesion burden and more advanced brain atrophy compared with healthy controls (HC). 8 Similarly, it is not uncommon to observe confounding etiologies of new white matter lesion development, such as migraine or cerebral small vessel disease, in radiologically active patients with MS in clinical practice. Therefore, devising improved methods of differentiating new inflammatory demyelinating MS lesions from lesions due to comorbid small vessel disease or migraine is of high clinical value. Understanding the lesion etiology has important ramifications for determining the need for DMT escalation, as this might be indicated in patients demonstrating breakthrough MS disease activity but not in patients with new non-MS white matter lesion development. The central vein sign (CVS) is a central linear hypointensity within lesions, visualized on susceptibility-sensitive MRI sequences (such as T2*-weighted scans) and corresponding to the small vein or venule around which the lesion formed. 9 , 10 The CVS has been proposed as a radiologic biomarker and is seen with high frequency in MS lesions, 11 , 12 such that it can effectively differentiate MS from other etiologies associated with nonspecific white matter lesions. 13 , 14 However, whereas the CVS has shown promise in aiding the initial diagnosis of MS based on the evaluation of established lesions, the CVS characteristics of newly appearing T2/FLAIR or Gd+ lesions in MS have not been comprehensively described. In this study, we sought to (1) investigate CVS characteristics of newly developing lesions in MS cases and HCs followed longitudinally; (2) study their relationship with clinical and radiologic measures of disease burden; and (3) describe the frequency of associated DMT changes seen retrospectively in this cohort.

extracted_data.document_summary: This 3-year longitudinal study characterized the central vein sign (CVS) profiles in newly developing white matter lesions in Multiple Sclerosis (MS) patients. It found that most new lesions were CVS+ (68%) and established that younger age and a higher baseline CVS+ percentage are associated with an increased likelihood of new CVS+ lesion development, thereby identifying CVS as a predictive radiologic biomarker for MS disease activity and informing clinical decisions.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study characterizing the Central Vein Sign (CVS) as a diagnostic imaging biomarker in the context of Multiple Sclerosis lesion development and progression.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This retrospective longitudinal cohort study followed adults with MS and healthy controls for a median of 3.1 years (Q1–Q3: 0.7–6.3 years). MRI scans were conducted on 3T Siemens or Philips scanners using specific submillimeter T2*-weighted, 3D millimetric T1-weighted MPRAGE/MP2RAGE, and 3D millimetric T2-weighted FLAIR sequences. The study did not involve specific therapeutic interventions or dose comparisons, though retrospective observations of disease-modifying therapy (DMT) changes were noted.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Brain white matter lesions (T2 and/or gadolinium-enhancing) detected via T2*-weighted MRI
analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Radiologic imaging characteristic (linear hypointensity) and classification (presence/absence of central vein within a lesion) via MRI

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: 68% (159/233) of new CVS-eligible lesions were CVS+. In gadolinium-enhancing (Gd+) lesions, the CVS+ percentage increased from 67% (102/152) at first observation to 82% (92/114) after a median follow-up of 2.8 years. Younger age (OR = 0.5 per 10-year increase, 95% CI = 0.3–0.8) and higher baseline CVS+ percentage (OR = 1.4-1.5 per 10% increase, 95% CI = 1.1–1.9) were associated with increased likelihood of new CVS+ lesion development. New juxta/leukocortical lesions showed a lower OR of CVS+ status (OR = 0.4, 95% CI = 0.2–0.8) compared to subcortical/deep white matter or periventricular lesions. Venular visibility was lower in Gd+ lesions but improved after enhancement/edema resolution.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Identifies a central linear hypointensity within lesions, corresponding to the small vein or venule around which the lesion formed, serving as an indicator of perivenular inflammation and demyelination, which are hallmarks of Multiple Sclerosis lesion pathology.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Newly developing T2 and/or gadolinium-enhancing white matter lesions in adults with Relapsing-Remitting MS (RRMS), Secondary Progressive MS (SPMS), Primary Progressive MS (PPMS), and Clinically Isolated Syndrome (CIS), observed during longitudinal follow-up; baseline CVS+ percentage as a prognostic factor for new lesion development.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Serves as a sensitive and specific radiologic biomarker for the diagnosis of Multiple Sclerosis, crucial for distinguishing MS lesions from other white matter lesions and understanding lesion pathogenesis. It is predictive of the risk of developing new CVS+ lesions over time, with its presence and development likelihood associated with patient age and baseline CVS status, thus informing clinical decisions regarding disease breakthrough and potential Disease-Modifying Therapy (DMT) escalation; new CVS- lesions may indicate other etiologies.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Newly developing Multiple Sclerosis lesions (detected via MRI)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Newly developing CVS+ lesions were larger than CVS− lesions (mean volume 59 vs 33 mm3, p < 0.001). An increased size of newly developing lesions was associated with a slightly higher likelihood of being CVS+ (OR 1.07 per each 10 mm3 increase in lesion volume, 95% CI 1.0–1.1).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Represents the physical extent of demyelination/inflammation in Multiple Sclerosis.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Larger lesion volume in MS typically indicates greater disease burden and potentially more significant neurological impact. In this study, it is associated with CVS+ status.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Cases with new lesions were younger (mean age 46 vs 51 years, p = 0.01). The likelihood of CVS+ lesion development increased with younger age (OR = 0.5 per 10-year increase in age, 95% CI = 0.3–0.8). Odds of any new CVS− lesion formation correlated with younger age at study inclusion (OR = 0.4, 95% CI = 0.2–0.8).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A demographic factor influencing disease susceptibility and progression in Multiple Sclerosis.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Risk factor for CVS-stratified new lesion formation in MS patients.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Younger age is a risk factor for developing new MS lesions, particularly CVS+ lesions, indicating higher disease activity.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Whole brain MRI assessment of MS patients
analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Imaging-based characteristic/predictor, quantified as a percentage of lesions that are CVS+.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Individuals with only new CVS+ lesions had a higher baseline CVS+ percentage compared with the other groups. The likelihood of CVS+ lesion development increased with higher baseline CVS+ percentage (OR = 1.5 per 10% increase in baseline CVS+ percentage, 95% CI = 1.1–1.9).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A diagnostic and prognostic imaging marker in Multiple Sclerosis, reflecting underlying venular inflammation.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Risk factor for CVS-stratified new lesion formation in MS patients.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Higher baseline CVS+ percentage is an indicator of ongoing disease activity and a predictor of future new CVS+ lesion formation.
